Industry influence/connections, personality details, known expansion opportunity, competitor tech stack, etc.) Notes: This customer had a rough start to implementation. They expected Aaron to tell them how to price and had no pricing method prepared. When asked how they currently priced their products, they didn't really know. They got frustrated about the export process, and thought that Aaron should be the Mozaik experts and not them. They didn't really understand their own software. But then things started to get much better implementation-wise. We were going strong for a few weeks, and then they just kept pushing meetings back because they got too busy. If they had clear documentation to start the process, I think we could have cut implementation time down by a month. Who's the main customer contact associated with this escalation? Ezra For reporting purposes, please check that this playbook is completed. Yes

Onboarding meeting #2 with Ezra and Michael (10/13/25) Review Stripe Connected? Triggers (enable Ezra and Michael to receive emails or texts for tasks) Review triggers Hiding categories to only show to verified customers? For testing, make sure to have a test account with a verified customer trigger. Today Price adjustments Financial settings Shipping Meeting Summary Josh and Michael discussed several key configuration areas within Allmoxy, focusing on tax setup, shipping preferences, financial workflows, and price adjustment mechanisms. The goal was to tailor Allmoxy for both B2B and consumer workflows, ensuring flexible payment handling, controlled shipping access, and pricing customization for various customer types. Key Takeaways Ezra’s Initial Questions Ezra created a test account but noticed sales tax wasn’t being calculated. It was later confirmed the system was correctly applying the 6% tax. Discussion arose around how Allmoxy handles tax-exempt customers. Michael mentioned Cornish had never charged sales tax and was exploring how to handle tax going forward. Josh clarified Allmoxy uses TaxJar for sales tax calculations, updating automatically based on customer or company zip codes unless a custom tax rate is applied. Shipping Michael asked how to restrict shipping for homeowners and require local pickup. Solution: Use tags (e.g., “homeowner”) to control which customers see specific shipping methods. Created a “Will Call” method only visible to users with the “homeowner” tag. Businesses can see both “Will Call” and standard delivery. Custom shipping formulas were implemented: <10 miles = $75 10–20 miles = $150 >20 miles = $250 Josh used ChatGPT to generate and test formulas for local delivery pricing. FedEx/UPS shipping integration is available but relies solely on weight, not dimensions. Price is returned from the carrier, and a multiplier (e.g., x2.3) is applied to estimate final charge. Recommendation: test average order weights to balance profitability and fairness. Financial Settings Allmoxy defaults to a “pay first” model, like Amazon. Michael expressed preference to offer limited credit to known local companies and default to prepayment for unknown or consumer customers. Options discussed: Use credit limits (e.g., $2,000) and build limits (e.g., $5,000) per company. Set defaults for all new customers and override for trusted accounts. Create tags like “local” or “verified” to govern payment terms. Trigger notifications for overdue payments and include terms in automated messages (e.g., full payment due before shipment). Payment methods: Stripe integration is used. It stores cards securely and allows repeat billing. ACH payments have lower fees. Stripe processing fees (~2.9%) can be offset with hidden price adjustments if needed. Invoices & QuickBooks: QuickBooks Online integration is in beta. In the meantime, use CSV export and third-party tools (e.g., Transaction Pro) to import Allmoxy data into QuickBooks. Manual journal entry is also a viable option for now. Price Adjustments Allmoxy supports automatic surcharges and discounts on a per-line-item basis. Adjustments can be: Global (e.g., 10% discount for all orders), Tag-based (e.g., surcharge for all “homeowner” accounts), Product-specific (e.g., MDF doors only), Company-specific (e.g., a discount for a trusted cabinet shop). Priority settings determine which adjustments apply if multiple are active. Suggestion: clean up inactive or unused price adjustments to reduce confusion. Price adjustments are not shown to customers if intended to offset fees (e.g., Stripe). Action Items Michael to review and confirm tax strategy with his new accountants, especially concerning tax exemption and resale scenarios. Create additional shipping methods as needed, tied to customer tags. Test and finalize the local delivery formula using known addresses. Set up default credit and build limits, and tag-based rules for verified vs. non-verified customers. Determine initial Stripe surcharge offset approach (e.g., via hidden price adjustment). Clean up old or inactive price adjustments in the system. Consider simple rules and low credit limits for new/unknown customers to mitigate risk. Monitor QuickBooks integration progress or explore third-party import tools in the meantime. Next Steps Internally align on credit policy for new vs. existing customers (e.g., default limits, pay-first tagging). Finalize shipping and delivery strategy for homeowner vs. business customers. Build task automation and triggers for overdue payments, order status, and onboarding. Revisit 3D Designer in January once deprecated, and assess new consumer-facing tools Allmoxy may release (e.g., Cabinet Portal). Gather Mosaic or Cabinet Vision files if participating in the developer raffle for file testing.

Onboarding meeting #1 with Ezra & Michael Triggers Trigger for Mosaic manual review will notify the internal team when products with a specific tag (e.g., “Mosaic Manual Check”) are included in an order. This is to flag attributes that cannot be imported directly into Mosaic. New company creation trigger will send an email alert to designated employees (e.g., Ezra and Michael) when a new company signs up. Verified order trigger will notify the customer when an order has been verified and can also send internal users an export file to drop into Mosaic. Welcome email trigger can be sent automatically upon account creation to outline next steps and expectations (e.g., “Please allow 24 hours for account verification”). A proposed trigger will automatically apply a “non-verified” tag to new companies, restricting their access until approved. Tags Product tags: Used to group products requiring special handling or triggering (e.g., for Mosaic manual imports). Company tags: "Verified Customer": Grants access to full catalog and standard pricing. "Non-Verified Customer": Default for all new accounts; limits access until reviewed. "Homeowner" and "Business": Used to segment product/category visibility. Category and product visibility can be controlled using the "company exclusive" setting with tags. Some products (e.g., MDF doors) may need to be duplicated to allow tailored visibility for homeowners vs. business customers. Tags can be used to apply different price adjustments based on customer type. Company Creation Customers will be allowed to create their own accounts rather than requiring manual setup. Upon signup, a company will: Be required to submit their EIN (configured as a custom field). Automatically receive a “non-verified” tag. Be hidden from all product categories unless verified. Admins will receive a notification via trigger upon each new company signup. Admins must manually review the company and change the tag from “non-verified” to “verified customer” if approved. Contact Creation Each company must have at least one associated contact. Admins can create individual contact profiles for employees or customers. Internal employees (e.g., shop staff) can be added with customized permission levels. Customers created manually must have “make payments” permission explicitly enabled. Login credentials (username and temporary password) can be created manually when adding a contact. Internal users can test contact permissions by logging into accounts directly using assigned credentials. Custom Fields A custom field for EIN Number was added to the company signup form. Field Name: EIN Number Variable Name: ein_number Set as required for new business account creation Field is editable and visible during sign-up Additional custom fields can be added as needed for internal qualification or filtering. Custom field responses will populate directly into the company’s contact page. Meeting Summary The team met with Josh Baker from Allmoxy to walk through account configuration, Mosaic export setup, product visibility management, and automation via tags and triggers. Key features were demonstrated and tested, including restricting catalog access for unverified customers, sending automated emails, and configuring shipping methods and Stripe payments. The goal was to finalize backend logic and begin internal testing of customer workflows and pricing configurations. Key Takeaways Important Discussions Product attributes were updated for MDF doors, slab doors, floating shelves, and applied panels. Mosaic exports are functioning for most product types; MDF and slab door exports still need testing. Tags and triggers will be used to manage visibility, approvals, and Mosaic import limitations. Front-end and pricing logic will be finalized before customer onboarding. Orders will be verified internally before being locked from customer edits and moved into production. Technical Issues & Fixes Applied panel pricing formulas were not saving properly; Aaron resolved this during the call. Audio issues at the beginning of the meeting were resolved by switching devices. Bid deletion process was clarified and demonstrated. Decisions Made Self-service account creation will be allowed but controlled using verification workflows. EIN will be required at signup to help distinguish businesses from homeowners. Verified customer tag will unlock full catalog visibility; non-verified customers will see no products. Stripe will be the payment processor; setup will begin soon. Products may be duplicated for different customer types where necessary. Challenges or Concerns Visibility setup using tags and duplication can become complex and needs careful testing. Search bar visibility for restricted products cannot currently be disabled. Stripe requires detailed company information and may delay payment processing if not set up early. Action Items Ezra to: Complete testing of Mosaic exports for MDF and slab doors. Set up and test product visibility rules using dummy accounts and tags. Finalize trigger for Mosaic import alert. Review and configure Stripe payment processing. Set up welcome email and new company alert triggers. Josh to: Send Allmoxy knowledge base/articles to Ezra. Assist with trigger and pricing formula setup as needed. Michael to: Align with Ezra on customer approval workflows and pricing structure. Review Stripe onboarding requirements. Next Steps Begin internal testing using dummy accounts with homeowner and business tag combinations. Finalize Stripe integration and run test transactions. Configure and test customer visibility, order flow, and trigger emails. Duplicate products and assign tag restrictions where needed for specific customer types. Continue exploring triggers, pricing adjustments, and process automation in next week’s session. Next follow-up meeting scheduled for Thursday with a focus on trigger implementation and potential launch preparation.

Canary & Allmoxy Sales Training Meeting Canary & Allmoxy Sales Training Meeting December 19, 2025 11:15 AM MST 25 mins sarah@allmoxy.com madison@allmoxy.com sales@canarycc.com ap@canarycc.com View Meeting Recording Customer Account Management and Tagging The team clarified the structured approach to customer account creation and tagging to ensure correct pricing and product visibility. Sarah Pierce outlined the account hierarchy where a company acts as an umbrella for multiple contacts, each requiring login access to Almoxy, with individual homeowner and retail customer accounts as alternatives (03:02) Contacts must be linked to their company to enable login and permission controls. Tags are critical for product availability and pricing, with Tony and Michelle responsible for tag management. Correct tagging ensures contractors and dealers see accurate pricing tiers and product selections. This tagging system directly supports differentiated customer experiences and revenue management. Financial settings were explained, including two checkout flows: pay before processing and credit limit, with recommended credit limits for new customers set between $5,000 and $10,000 (06:27) Pay before processing requires payment before orders reach ordered status, controlling cash flow upfront. Credit limit allows orders up to a set limit before payment, keeping the order pipeline active without upfront payments. Order limits typically exceed credit limits to permit multiple pending orders before payment clears. Grace periods and finance charges are configured to enforce timely payments and manage receivables risk. Order Entry and Folder Organization Order entry processes were optimized for speed and clarity using order-level settings and folder structures to improve client experience and internal handling. Sarah introduced order-level settings that allow global attribute changes (like closet color) across all products in an order, reducing manual updates for customers and sales reps (12:41) Customers can apply changes globally or selectively to new products, streamlining order edits. Folder-level settings extend this control to subsets of products, helping differentiate sections within larger orders. This feature supports faster quote revisions and customization, enhancing client satisfaction. Sarah planned to send supporting articles for further training on these features. Folders act as an organizational tool to divide large orders by space or project segments, such as separating closets or kitchen components, with subtotaling at the folder level improving bid clarity (15:19) Folders enable clients to view and manage the order in manageable segments, improving transparency. Sarah noted potential production implications as folders may split similar product lines, which needs confirmation from Tony to avoid disrupting cut lists. The team agreed the client-side clarity outweighs potential production complexities, pending testing. The folder feature was identified as a solution to client confusion with long, undifferentiated parts lists. Reporting and Sales Visibility The discussion highlighted report usage for sales tracking and commission attribution, emphasizing the need for accurate tagging and order status management. Sarah emphasized that sales reports depend on orders reaching the “status to charge customer,” which varies by client and can affect report reliability (20:19) Some customers are charged at different order statuses, causing timing discrepancies in sales data. Orders report allows filtering by entered date and tags, enabling sales reps to track their orders and commission-related activity. Tagging customers or orders with sales reps’ identifiers is essential for accurate commission tracking and sales attribution. Product tagging can also track push efforts on specific items by filtering orders containing those products. Invoice reports provide comprehensive financial visibility including credit card fees and finance charges, supporting broader accounting and revenue management needs (22:50) Sales focus remains primarily on orders and sales reports, with less emphasis on aging and collections reports for the sales team. The reporting capabilities support performance monitoring and strategic sales efforts. Integration and Workflow Alignment The team confirmed current workflow integration between design and order systems, supporting smooth data transfer and order management. The team confirmed Tony and Michelle handle exports from Closet Pro to Almoxy and export order data as needed for Excel and other reports (23:50) This integrated workflow supports seamless transition from design to order entry without redundant data entry. Exported data supports downstream operational needs such as production planning and financial reconciliation. Continued coordination between sales, design, and operations teams is implied to maintain data accuracy and efficiency. The process supports scalability and reduces errors in order processing. Training and Knowledge Transfer The meeting focused on foundational training for new team members to ensure consistent use of Almoxy and enable effective sales operations. Sarah and Madison committed to sending detailed articles covering folders, order-level settings, company creation, and contact creation to support Melissa’s onboarding (24:20) This training material aims to unify workflows and reduce inconsistent practices across the team. Melissa’s intention to blend different user approaches into an optimized personal workflow was acknowledged as positive. Ongoing support remains accessible through Madison for clarification and advanced questions. The materials and follow-up will improve onboarding speed and operational consistency. Action Items Sarah Pierce Send training articles on folders, order-level settings, company creation, and contact creation to Melissa for further review. (24:20) Melissa Discuss folder usage and potential production impact with Tony to ensure it does not disrupt production workflow. (18:10) Communicate with Tony and Michelle regarding tagging structure and financial settings to confirm accuracy and consistency. Retention Meeting October 2024 In attendance: Broc, Kenzi, Chesky Chesky has fallen off the wagon for months with attempting engagements and has been unresponsive. He was very disgruntled in the spring and we turned off his payment.  In the spring he said that he wanted to continue to try to make Allmoxy work and Kenzi reached out several times without him showing up. He randomly booked the retention meeting without reaching out providing the purpose behind the meeting. Goal: to understand where the partnership would be valuable moving forward, create an action plan that makes sense. Chesky is trying not to have customers enter all parts through Allmoxy because they get frustrated. The shop benefits from it but for customers it is a pain the neck. When you have a couple thousand parts to enter it's very time consuming. The way that Allmoxy prices things is very good, you can have a base price, a square footage price but the part he is looking for is the backend office materials, etc. and it comes down to price and what it will cost and take time wise to get setup and see if it's worth it. Essentially wanting a scope for next steps to see where it would take them and what it would look like. Chesky mentioned that he wanted to see how other closet manufacturing shops utilize Allmoxy. Broc feels like there are a lot of variables when it comes to that. And he is unable to show others who are using it. But when he can say is that there are other closet shops that use it for parts and kits (more of a sku'd product) and things like he does and does it successfully. But Chesky does custom closets. They are either having clients do either one of two things. Either having their clients create the order on the front end, or they're allowing almoxy to take client data through an import CSV file and upload it into almoxy. He currently exports out of closet pro and into closet vision. It isn't completely accurate. When they import into closet vision they are able to see it pretty well and tweak it to what it needs to be. Whereas with Allmoxy all he sees is parts. He doesn't know where and what to tweak and it get's confusing. Sarah and Juan would be the best people to ask what solutions there are as they are in thick of it with our customers and can better speak to what that looks like. Without Allmoxy what are the alternatives in your mind? Chesky said build something from scratch but he doesn't want to do that. We don't want them to do that either. What do you see the value of Allmoxy being for dollar wise? The deal we gave him was $899 a month. Our base price is $1099. If Allmoxy is not the main software he isn't sure if he wants to pursue it or not. He is getting in a lot of orders. Inventory, purchasing, etc. are a pain point from him. He wants to make it as simple as possible. What Chesky needs: To understand what is the best way for customers to come into closet pro without customers going through 800 parts. Second, see how much time and money it would take to build the back end of the office functionality side of things such as inventory and pricing etc. We should be able to get this back to him beginning of next week. He could get on Monday or Tuesday. Broc is scheduling a scope call. Chesky said if he doesn't hop on to please call him and remind him to hop on. The catalog isn't laid out super well right now. The way closet pro is laid out is in sections not by parts. Chesky showed us a demo of closet pro/cabinet vision and what it looks like and said he would be willing to show a demo of what it looks like on the scoping call to help us better understand the full picture. Next steps: Get on a no cost scope call with services team with Sarah and Juan since Sarah understands the closet side of things very very well. Broc booked a time for Chesky and team next week. engagements.title: Wurth LAC: Track Slide-A-Shelf B2B go-live
engagements.body: Per the 6/10/26 meeting, Slide-A-Shelf products are built but marked unavailable pending markup from Jeremy Mitchell and Carson's system config. Confirm the markup is finalized, products are toggled live and Chris and Mary are onboarded. Keep launch momentum. Source: note 6/10/26.

6/10/26 - Wurth and Slide-A-Shelf Meeting - https://app.fireflies.ai/view/Slide-A-Shelf-Wurth-LAC-Allmoxy-B2B-Meeting::01KT07QD6PTM5VE5K1F2VAQW6M Agenda: Both parties to determine markup and make products available Are we doing any price adjustment? (surcharge of any kind) Turn products to available Discuss next steps of Wurth's current internal processing of B2B orders to align with Slide-a-shelf's operations. Notes: Chris Godinez - joined since Mary couldn't make it due to family issues. Meeting Summary B2B partnership call between Slide-A-Shelf, Wurth LAC, and Allmoxy to align on pricing strategy, order processing workflows, system configuration, and pre-launch requirements Slide-A-Shelf products are built and integrated into Wurth's Allmoxy platform but are currently marked unavailable pending final pricing and markup decisions Meeting covered the full order lifecycle from customer placement through Wurth verification, PO entry, and Slide-A-Shelf production Leadership approval from Wurth's CEO and directors identified as a required step before the partnership goes live System configuration tasks assigned to Carson Ward, with follow-up items distributed across Slide-A-Shelf and Wurth teams Key Takeaways Important Discussions Slide-A-Shelf offers custom pullout shelves as direct-ship products through Wurth's platform, targeting cabinet makers and contractors who prefer not to build their own Wurth will use Allmoxy as the ordering and PO management platform; customers place orders through Wurth, Wurth verifies and enters POs, and Slide-A-Shelf downloads confirmed orders for production Slide-A-Shelf's 30-year brand history and product quality cited as key competitive advantages over brands such as Rev-A-Shelf New side-mount product includes rear sockets as an upgrade; an undermount version is in development and expected to launch first through Wurth Expansion opportunity identified: Slide-A-Shelf products could be promoted to cabinet manufacturers such as Lewis Cabinet Specialties and Timberline Cabinets, though all orders must flow through Wurth's system Orders for Slide-A-Shelf products mixed with other vendors must be split; customers should be directed to place separate orders per vendor to avoid fulfillment issues Technical Issues and Fixes Slide-A-Shelf products are currently visible internally to Wurth's team only and must be toggled to live after markup is finalized Carson confirmed the system supports a flat fee or percentage surcharge applied uniformly across all Slide-A-Shelf products as a placeholder markup Granular per-product pricing adjustments are possible but a standard markup is preferred as the starting point Email notification triggers can be configured to alert Wurth's team when a Slide-A-Shelf product order is placed, enabling order monitoring and split management Chris requested different status bubble colors for verified orders; Carson will investigate expanding color options Carson will set up Chris Codinez and Mary as contacts in the Wurth Slide-A-Shelf Allmoxy account for order verification and PO entry access Shipping charges and product costs are currently combined on invoices; separating them for accounting clarity is under discussion; Carson confirmed system flexibility to support either format Decisions Made Wurth customers will pay shipping separately at checkout; pricing strategy must account for freight costs to remain competitive Jamie Brinker will send Wurth wholesale costs, suggested retail prices, MAP pricing, and shipping cost details; Jeremy Mitchell's pricing manager will use this data to finalize the markup percentage Carson will implement the agreed markup in Wurth's Allmoxy system once confirmed Orders requiring measurement confirmation for six or more shelves will include a phone follow-up from Slide-A-Shelf to reduce costly errors All order price or measurement adjustments must be documented via email approval to maintain invoicing integrity A Slide-A-Shelf-branded letter, installation instructions, and hardware documentation will be included in shipments to Wurth customers; Worth branding adjustments are under review A dedicated support line for Wurth's Slide-A-Shelf customers has been established Carson will maintain a single email thread with all participants to centralize communication Challenges or Concerns Pricing must be set carefully to avoid Wurth's site listing products above Slide-A-Shelf's own retail pricing, which could cause customers to bypass Wurth Shipping costs are a complicating factor; unlike large retailers offering free shipping, Wurth customers will pay freight, which affects perceived competitiveness High product variability (over 15,000 variations) and custom measurement requirements create order accuracy risk; phone verification for larger orders is a current mitigation Brand naming on Wurth's platform requires care to avoid alienating other customers who may sell competing products Final approval from Wurth's CEO and directors is required before going live; Jeremy Mitchell will coordinate this review after pricing and documentation are finalized Action Items Jamie Brinker: Provide Wurth with Slide-A-Shelf wholesale costs, suggested retail prices, MAP pricing, and shipping cost details Jamie Brinker: Share the current thank-you letter draft and installation instructions with Wurth for potential branding adjustments Jamie Brinker: Coordinate internally to manage order adjustments with proper email approvals for price or measurement changes Jamie Brinker: Follow up with Stephanie and the accounting team regarding possible invoice format changes to separate shipping from product costs for Wurth Jeremy Mitchell: Determine the appropriate markup or surcharge to apply on Slide-A-Shelf products in Wurth's system, then communicate pricing strategy and margins to Slide-A-Shelf and the internal pricing team Jeremy Mitchell: Coordinate with CEO and directors for final review and approval of pricing, packaging, and partnership details before going live Jeremy Mitchell: Obtain and share Quality Craft paperwork with the Slide-A-Shelf and Wurth teams to ensure consistent documentation Chris Codinez: Collaborate with Jamie and Carson to finalize paperwork and PO processes, verify orders on Allmoxy, and add POs accordingly Chris Codinez: Provide examples of invoices and packing slips used with current vendors to Slide-A-Shelf for review and replication Chris Codinez: Test and confirm Allmoxy site access and order processing capabilities for Wurth Slide-A-Shelf users Carson Ward: Implement pricing adjustment setup on Wurth's Allmoxy system for Slide-A-Shelf products with ability to apply a uniform surcharge or discount, keeping open the option for granular adjustments if needed Carson Ward: Configure system triggers and notifications to alert Wurth's team of orders containing Slide-A-Shelf products and order status changes Carson Ward: Assist Wurth team contacts (Chris and Mary) with Allmoxy access setup for order verification and purchase order entry Carson Ward: Follow up with Chris and Mary on documentation workflows and integrate required paperwork automation in Allmoxy Carson Ward: Distribute meeting recording and summary notes to all participants and maintain a shared communication thread for updates Next Steps Pricing markup percentage to be confirmed by Jeremy Mitchell's pricing manager after receiving cost data from Jamie Brinker; Carson to implement in Allmoxy once confirmed Wurth products to be toggled live in Allmoxy after markup is finalized and system configuration is complete Paperwork and documentation formats to be aligned between Wurth, Slide-A-Shelf, and Quality Craft to replicate current vendor workflows Order notification triggers to be configured and tested in Allmoxy Wurth contacts (Chris Codinez and Mary) to be onboarded with Allmoxy access in the coming days Jeremy Mitchell to present full pricing, packaging, and partnership details to Wurth's CEO and directors for final approval prior to launch Marketing collateral and customer communication materials (literature, QR code cards, branded inserts) to be prepared by Slide-A-Shelf for inclusion in shipments following leadership approval Additional calls to be scheduled as needed to resolve outstanding questions before go-live

engagements.body: Rugby & Allmoxy | B2B Connection

12/11/25 - Onboarding Meeting (Meet with Evolve) https://app.fireflies.ai/view/FW-Allmoxy-Evolve-Cabinet::01KC2EF6N2XAJYWZ7A04G5QGSH Meeting Summary The meeting centered around the integration and setup of Stanley's custom door products within the Allmoxy platform for Rugby to resell. Discussions covered remaining technical issues, product setup steps, pricing configuration, materials management, and shipping logistics. A phased rollout strategy was proposed, including a plan to finalize configurations before the end of the year, with potential go-live in early 2025. Key Takeaways Important Discussions Stanley is waiting for Allmoxy to resolve a pricing issue related to panel thickness before proceeding with catalog sharing. The issue centers on mispricing the quarter-inch center door panel as a three-quarter-inch panel, affecting cost accuracy. A new material line (Tafisa from Rugby) will be added, but only once current pricing issues are resolved. Stanley clarified that Rugby customers should only see materials Rugby stocks, to avoid unsupported orders (e.g., Wilson Art in some markets). Custom product setup for Rugby’s instance will be handled through cloned versions of Stanley’s existing products, with limited material selections shown. Discussion around controlling the user experience: avoiding overwhelming material dropdowns and maintaining clean product presentation. Technical Issues & Fixes Current technical problem: Allmoxy misprices quarter-inch door panels as three-quarter-inch. Solution: Either document changes to send to Aaron for implementation, or set up a direct meeting with Aaron for a collaborative adjustment session. Future product flexibility depends on setting up accurate material depth attributes (e.g., panel thickness) and logic to avoid material bloat in user selections. Custom shipping weight (dim weight) must be manually input due to system limitations. Decisions Made Stanley will hold off on adding Rugby materials until the panel pricing fix is completed. Stanley will enable products for B2B resale once pricing is accurate, and Rugby will then pull them into their instance. Products for Rugby will be cloned and limited to Rugby-approved materials only. A single universal price adjustment will be used for all B2B products (instead of multiple per product). Future customer-specific attributes will be enabled when available to eliminate the need for cloned products. Local delivery will be handled by Rugby for nearby customers, and out-of-region freight will be managed directly by Stanley. Challenges or Concerns Risk of Rugby customers selecting unavailable or unreleased materials (e.g., Tafisa color not in the U.S.). Laminating veneer to match stock colors for quarter-inch panels is unreliable due to color variation. Teams issues on Stanley's end prevented screen sharing for product configuration during the meeting. Shipping complexity due to lack of integrated freight calculation (dim weight must be added manually). Action Items Stanley to: Finalize pricing corrections in Allmoxy for quarter-inch vs. three-quarter-inch panels. Provide list of products to be cloned and prepared for Rugby’s instance. Await Brandon’s list of stocked Tafisa SKUs (both quarter-inch and three-quarter-inch). Work with Carson to schedule a meeting with Aaron next week for pricing logic finalization. Brandon Anderson to: Send list of Tafisa materials stocked at Rugby. Carson Ward to: Coordinate the engineering meeting with Aaron and Stanley. Guide Stanley through enabling B2B product sharing via Allmoxy. Support configuration of cloned products with limited attributes for Rugby. Josh & Rugby Team to: Prepare for eventual integration of Allmoxy instance into the Rugby website (iframe or direct link). Test the ordering process once Stanley's catalog is ready. Next Steps Carson to send Aaron’s availability for a pricing review and configuration session with Stanley. 12/11/25 - Onboarding Meeting (Meet with Evolve) https://app.fireflies.ai/view/FW-Allmoxy-Evolve-Cabinet::01KC2EF6N2XAJYWZ7A04G5QGSH Meeting Summary The meeting centered around the integration and setup of Stanley's custom door products within the Allmoxy platform for Rugby to resell. Discussions covered remaining technical issues, product setup steps, pricing configuration, materials management, and shipping logistics. A phased rollout strategy was proposed, including a plan to finalize configurations before the end of the year, with potential go-live in early 2025. Key Takeaways Important Discussions Stanley is waiting for Allmoxy to resolve a pricing issue related to panel thickness before proceeding with catalog sharing. The issue centers on mispricing the quarter-inch center door panel as a three-quarter-inch panel, affecting cost accuracy. A new material line (Tafisa from Rugby) will be added, but only once current pricing issues are resolved. Stanley clarified that Rugby customers should only see materials Rugby stocks, to avoid unsupported orders (e.g., Wilson Art in some markets). Custom product setup for Rugby’s instance will be handled through cloned versions of Stanley’s existing products, with limited material selections shown. Discussion around controlling the user experience: avoiding overwhelming material dropdowns and maintaining clean product presentation. Technical Issues & Fixes Current technical problem: Allmoxy misprices quarter-inch door panels as three-quarter-inch. Solution: Either document changes to send to Aaron for implementation, or set up a direct meeting with Aaron for a collaborative adjustment session. Future product flexibility depends on setting up accurate material depth attributes (e.g., panel thickness) and logic to avoid material bloat in user selections. Custom shipping weight (dim weight) must be manually input due to system limitations. Decisions Made Stanley will hold off on adding Rugby materials until the panel pricing fix is completed. Stanley will enable products for B2B resale once pricing is accurate, and Rugby will then pull them into their instance. Products for Rugby will be cloned and limited to Rugby-approved materials only. A single universal price adjustment will be used for all B2B products (instead of multiple per product). Future customer-specific attributes will be enabled when available to eliminate the need for cloned products. Local delivery will be handled by Rugby for nearby customers, and out-of-region freight will be managed directly by Stanley. Challenges or Concerns Risk of Rugby customers selecting unavailable or unreleased materials (e.g., Tafisa color not in the U.S.). Laminating veneer to match stock colors for quarter-inch panels is unreliable due to color variation. Teams issues on Stanley's end prevented screen sharing for product configuration during the meeting. Shipping complexity due to lack of integrated freight calculation (dim weight must be added manually). Action Items Stanley to: Finalize pricing corrections in Allmoxy for quarter-inch vs. three-quarter-inch panels. Provide list of products to be cloned and prepared for Rugby’s instance. Await Brandon’s list of stocked Tafisa SKUs (both quarter-inch and three-quarter-inch). Work with Carson to schedule a meeting with Aaron next week for pricing logic finalization. Brandon Anderson to: Send list of Tafisa materials stocked at Rugby. Carson Ward to: Coordinate the engineering meeting with Aaron and Stanley. Guide Stanley through enabling B2B product sharing via Allmoxy. Support configuration of cloned products with limited attributes for Rugby. Josh & Rugby Team to: Prepare for eventual integration of Allmoxy instance into the Rugby website (iframe or direct link). Test the ordering process once Stanley's catalog is ready. Next Steps Carson to send Aaron’s availability for a pricing review and configuration session with Stanley. Stanley to complete product setup and confirm pricing accuracy before cloning Rugby-specific versions. Rugby team to test ordering through Stanley’s instance once products and pricing are finalized. Determine shipping strategy per region: local via Rugby; freight handled by Stanley with manual input. Evaluate if temporary direct-link access can be used instead of iframe for faster Rugby launch. Target: Internal testing by January 1, 2025; public launch potentially by March 1, 2025.

Title: Allmoxy Demo - : The Job Shop Date: Wed Jul 23 2025 17:45:00 GMT-0400 (Eastern Daylight Time) Participants: bobby@allmoxy.com, info@thejobshopco.com, dave@thejobshopco.com Transcript: See full transcript Audio: Listen to audio Duration: 45 mins Overview - Bobby Lewis conducted the Allmoxy demo for The Job Shop, a cabinet shop aiming for $500K annual drawer box spending from five key Manhattan clients. - The Job Shop received a referral from a Manhattan client generating $7.5 million annually in residential casework, highlighting potential growth opportunities. - Allmoxy's customer portal allows self-service ordering, tracking, and integrates Stripe for payments at 2.9%, saving 0.6% compared to QuickBooks' 3.5%. - The inventory management system features automated tracking and allocation of materials, ensuring efficient production aligned with order verification. - Bobby's previous experience demonstrated Allmoxy's effectiveness, reducing accounts receivable aging from 62 days to 14 days on 30-day terms. - Project scheduling and Gantt chart features are prioritized for development in 2025 to enhance production planning capabilities. - Full API integration with Zapier is available, allowing connectivity with third-party tools for improved scheduling and task management. - The pricing structure involves a monthly subscription based on annual revenue processed, with an implementation cost of $300-400 for setup. - A hybrid build approach was recommended for The Job Shop, facilitating client learning alongside the implementation engineer for better formula writing. - Ongoing support includes a dedicated customer success representative within the subscription plan to assist with product configuration and troubleshooting. Notes 📋 Initial Context & Introduction Bobby Lewis conducting Allmoxy software demo from Vegas trade show for The Job Shop, a small cabinet shop in Hellertown, Pennsylvania. The Job Shop specializes in custom drawer boxes and received referral from Manhattan client doing $7.5 million in residential casework annually. Client requested they use Allmoxy for billing and payment processing for drawer box orders. The Job Shop targeting five major players in Manhattan market, with potential $500K annual drawer box spending per client. Company uses Mosaic CNC for cabinetry and Kantec dovetail machines for drawer boxes. 💻 Software Overview & Customer Portal Allmoxy creates branded customer portal at company.allmoxy.com with custom logos and optional custom domain. Customer self-service portal allows clients to place orders, see pricing, and track delivery dates Amazon-style. Integrated Stripe payment processing at 2.9% rate vs QuickBooks' 3.5% rate, saving 0.6% on credit card transactions. QuickBooks integration in beta for seamless transaction sync. System includes drawer box templates ready for implementation. Automated triggers send customer notifications for order confirmations, shipping updates, and completion notices. 📦 Inventory Management & Production Features Barcode scanning system for tracking products through production with printable labels for drawer boxes. Supply system tracks inventory automatically, allocating materials when orders verified and comparing against minimum quantities. Work schedule management organizes production by delivery dates with start/stop job tracking. System can generate packing slips, invoices, and shipping reports automatically. Tax Jar integration calculates appropriate tax rates by customer location. Bobby's previous experience: managed $1.6 million monthly production with one secretary using Allmoxy. 🚀 Advanced Features & Development Roadmap Project scheduling and Gantt chart functionality identified as 2025 development priority. Full API integration available with Zapier connectivity for third-party calendar and scheduling systems. System supports customer-specific pricing with granular discounts by company tags or individual products. Cabinet operation scaling available beyond drawer boxes for dealers wanting manufactured parts. Money collection improvement: Bobby's experience showed reduction from 62-day to 14-day average aging on 30-day terms. 💰 Pricing Structure & Implementation Timeline Monthly subscription model based on annual revenue processed through system, locked for 12 months then adjusted based on actual usage. Implementation cost: approximately $300-400 for 2 sessions with implementation engineer for drawer box setup. Customer success representative included in subscription for ongoing support. Setup timeline: estimated 2 hours for simple solid maple dovetail drawer box product configuration. Hybrid build approach recommended where client learns formula writing alongside implementation engineer. Agenda: Review pricing sheet provided Talk about materials and attribute selections Confirm where Evan and Marques need to enter data for pricing to start calculating. Meeting Summary The meeting involved Carson Ward, Evan, Marques B, and Aaron Dundas reviewing the pricing structure setup in Allmoxy. Evan is transitioning into the primary role of managing Allmoxy-related tasks, while Marques focuses on Cabinet Vision and CNC processes. The goal was to clarify the labor and material pricing logic within Allmoxy, validate current formulas, and empower Evan and Marques to configure and manage pricing independently. Key Takeaways Important Discussions Role Assignments: Evan will manage Allmoxy pricing and configuration going forward; Marques will handle Cabinet Vision and CNC-related tasks. Pricing Formula Structure: Labor and material pricing were discussed in depth, focusing on clarity, customization, and future flexibility. Casework pricing (base, tall, wall, vanity) is calculated using lineal footage multiplied by labor rates. Door pricing is based on square footage, with fallback minimums for small door sizes. Drawer box types (e.g., dovetail, rollout) have differentiated labor costs. Use of Allmoxy Meta Attributes: Meta attributes were introduced to assign custom labor rates based on cabinet type and product characteristics. These attributes allow scalable, global pricing changes and keep labor logic clean and consistent. Meta values must be manually added to each product and defaulted to appropriate values (e.g., “base”, “wall”). Material and Hardware Costing: Pricing tables can include hardware like Blum Tandem glides. Material pricing factors include square footage, waste percentage, and margin settings. Rollout and drawer box labor included separately from material. Technical Issues & Fixes Missing data in the shared pricing sheet (e.g., door per sheet data line) was clarified and corrected. Some final square footage calculations (e.g., for slab doors) didn’t save in the spreadsheet but were resolved in discussion. Proxy formulas were built and tested during the session for pricing logic. Clarification was provided on how Allmoxy handles deleted attributes and their permanent reservation. Decisions Made Use Meta attributes for labor assignment across product categories. Price slab doors at $25/sq ft, painted MDF slab doors at $60/sq ft, and five-piece painted MDF doors at $75/sq ft. Set a fallback labor price of $40/door for doors under 1.5 sq ft. Casework labor rates: Base: $125/lineal ft Tall: $250/lineal ft Drawer box labor: Dovetail: $175 Standard: $20 Rollouts: $120 Glide cost will be included directly in pricing using existing tables since standard hardware is always used. Challenges or Concerns Evan requested further clarification and training on how attributes and pricing formulas function in Allmoxy. Awareness was raised about the irreversible nature of attribute names in Allmoxy and the cascading effects of deleting them. Marques noted uncertainty about integrating laminated five-piece door options, which remain under development. There’s some need for future enhancement around installation pricing visibility and material tracking (e.g., sheet usage). Action Items Carson to send the Zoom recording and transcript for reference. Evan to review the recording and begin hands-on input of materials, attributes, and pricing adjustments in Allmoxy. Marques to provide updated pricing numbers for painted MDF slabs and five-piece doors and help configure new product types. Aaron to finalize proxy formulas and push them to all relevant product types once meta attributes are assigned. Evan & Marques to attach and default meta attributes to all relevant cabinet products in the catalog. Next Steps Evan and Marques to independently input data and test pricing logic in Allmoxy. Once comfortable, they’ll reach out to Carson to schedule a follow-up session. Carson will coordinate availability with Aaron for the next review session, potentially the following week or last week of May depending on progress. 4/8/26 - Check-in Meeting - https://app.fireflies.ai/view/Urbania-Cabinets-Allmoxy::01KN7WWFX9SQPKW3KWRDED2H3E Agenda: Pricing check in (Where's Gabriel at?) Meeting Summary Check-in call between Gabriel and Carson to revisit the Allmoxy catalog setup and address ongoing blockers preventing progress. Gabriel expressed significant frustration with internal indecision — the team has been shifting focus between custom residential and commercial cabinet work week to week with no clear direction. The conversation resulted in a clear, simplified path forward: use the existing Allmoxy template catalog as the foundation, apply Stevens Wood colors, and define pricing attributes for all base products. Gabriel committed to setting aside previous distractions (including the Texas company SKU catalog) and focusing exclusively on the agreed-upon approach. Key Takeaways Important Discussions Gabriel's team has been unable to make consistent decisions about whether to focus on custom residential cabinets or commercial work, which has stalled all Allmoxy catalog progress. General contractors in their target market are not expected to sit down and configure complex orders online — the catalog needs to be fast, simple, and price-transparent so that a GC can get a number in under five minutes. Gabriel wants to move away from acting as a reseller of third-party cabinet lines and instead focus on their own production with a straightforward pricing model. Gabriel acknowledged internal misalignment on pricing — one team member thinks $160 per cabinet is right, another is thinking closer to $900. This needs to be resolved before catalog pricing can be defined. Carson clarified that Allmoxy supports multiple pricing structures: per-unit/box pricing with a multiplier, or square footage cost plus markup with waste/yield factors. The team needs to decide which model fits their operation. Carson shared the Allmoxy Knowledge Base pricing documentation to help Gabriel and his team work through the pricing structure decision independently before the next meeting. Technical Issues and Fixes The Texas company SKU catalog Gabriel had previously shared was set aside — it is an existing online catalog that Gabriel can handle with a simple multiplier (approximately 0.45) when needed. It will not be incorporated into the Allmoxy catalog build. No engineering hours have been spent yet, which means there is no sunk cost and no need to undo prior work — the project is still in a clean starting position. Decisions Made Move forward using the existing Allmoxy template catalog as the foundation — no custom catalog build at this time. Apply Stevens Wood color/texture options as the initial finish offering. Include all base cabinet products from the template. Set aside all other catalog considerations and external SKU data for now. Gabriel will review the Allmoxy pricing documentation Carson sent and organize his pricing logic (attributes, cost model, per-unit or square footage approach) before the next meeting. Challenges or Concerns Internal team alignment remains the primary blocker — without a consistent direction from leadership, catalog work cannot be finalized. Pricing consensus does not yet exist within Gabriel's team, which must be resolved before Allmoxy engineering can configure the catalog. Gabriel noted that the ongoing scope changes and unresolved decisions have been mentally overwhelming and have prevented him from moving forward. Action Items Gabriel — Review the Allmoxy pricing documentation shared by Carson and organize pricing logic for base cabinet products, including: preferred pricing model (per unit vs. square footage), attribute options to include at launch (e.g., door type, drawer front, box material, finish), and any per-attribute upcharges or sub-calculations needed. Gabriel — Align with his team internally on a single pricing model and per-cabinet price range before the next meeting. Carson — Send Gabriel the recording from this meeting along with relevant Allmoxy Knowledge Base articles on pricing structures and catalog setup. Next Steps Carson to send the meeting recording and resource links following this call. Gabriel to send organized pricing information and attribute details to Carson by approximately the following Monday. Carson to follow up via email Monday to confirm receipt and schedule a follow-up Zoom meeting for mid-week (Wednesday or as available). Next meeting goal: review Gabriel's pricing data and begin configuring the template catalog with defined attributes and pricing logic.

Set up Stripe for payment processing Create a test account and contact Create a test order Meeting Summary Continued working session to define SKU structure, product groupings, and pricing logic for cabinet catalog build. Focused on organizing base cabinet SKUs into clear product groupings (e.g., Base Two Drawer, Base Three Drawer, Base Open, Blind Corner). Discussed how SKUs should be grouped and how they will appear on the order page. Clarified differences between Shaker and Slab door offerings, including customization capabilities. Reviewed current spreadsheet structure and pricing columns to align on true cost, markup, and retail strategy. Identified need to clearly define pricing rules before engineering begins catalog construction. Agreed to document finish pricing logic, door style availability, and slab width modification rules. Scheduled next working session to review finalized logic and structure. Key Takeaways Product Grouping Structure SKUs must be grouped cleanly into logical product categories (e.g., Base Two Drawer, Base Three Drawer, Base Open, Blind Corner). Engineers need clear SKU-to-product mappings before building the catalog. Some SKUs (e.g., spice pull-out, trash pull-out, full height door variants) may require recategorization. Shaker vs. Slab Configuration Shaker cabinets: Locked to fixed SKU sizes (typically 3-inch increments). Width, height, and depth are not customizable. Slab cabinets: Width can be customized. Custom widths must follow a pricing rule that references the next highest SKU price bracket. Customization logic must be fully defined before build begins. Slab Width Pricing Logic (Proposed) Slab cabinets can be ordered at any width. If the width is below or equal to the base SKU size, pricing remains at that SKU’s minimum price. If width exceeds a SKU bracket, pricing rounds up to the next SKU tier. Specific width ranges (e.g., 25–26 inches vs. 27–29 inches) must be formally documented. Finish Pricing Rules Finish categories: Solid Colors: 10% upcharge Stains: 15% upcharge These percentage adjustments apply on top of base SKU pricing. Finish availability must clearly indicate whether it applies to: Shaker Slab Both Texture melamine should be included as a finish category and mapped to applicable door styles. Pricing Structure Clarifications “Retail price” column currently reflects reference pricing from supplier website. “Dealer sale price” represents base cost of goods. Moving forward: Use true cost as the foundation. Apply markup and finish adjustments through structured pricing logic. Retail discounts can later be handled via price adjustments rather than altering base formulas. Online pricing column will be treated as reference only. Engineering Readiness Before engineers begin: All SKU groupings must be finalized. Finish rules and door style availability must be clearly defined. Slab width modification rules must be explicitly written out. Retroactively modifying catalog logic after build would create significant additional work. Action Items Gabriel: Finalize and document SKU groupings by product category. Define slab width pricing brackets and rounding rules in detail. Confirm finish categories (Solid, Stain, Texture Melamine) and map availability to Shaker and Slab. Complete pricing rule documentation in the shared sheet before next meeting. Carson: Send meeting recording and recap summary. Prepare for engineering discussion once pricing and grouping logic is finalized. Next Steps Gabriel to focus on completing pricing logic and slab customization rules before the next session. Once logic is finalized, schedule a meeting with engineering to review structure and confirm implementation approach. Next working session scheduled for Friday the 27th at the same time.

02/12/26 - Onboarding Meeting - https://app.fireflies.ai/view/Urbania-Cabinets-Allmoxy-Catch-Up::01KH4FZTSKJ7ZAHJSXCG7G44VP Agenda: Review the product documentation that Gabriel provided Need to breakdown pricing more unless we're strictly going with a SKU model. Go over financial settings and customer account creation Next steps Schedule an implementation meeting to share the documentation with our team and see what questions each side has. Continue with platform training as implementation begins. Notes: Meeting Summary Reviewed SKU-based cabinet catalog structure for Shaker products sourced from an external supplier. Discussed pricing structure including dealer cost, markup, and handling fee. Clarified differences between Shaker (supplier-based, fixed SKUs) and Slab/3DL (in-house, customizable) product lines. Confirmed goal to launch a “plug-and-play” SKU catalog first for quick ordering scenarios. Discussed future phase for custom cabinetry with adjustable dimensions and expanded options. Agreed to refine SKU spreadsheet with clearer definitions and dimensional standards before engineering handoff. Scheduled follow-up meeting for next week at the same time. Key Takeaways Important Discussions Shaker cabinets: Pre-built, flat-pack cabinets from a supplier in Texas. Fully SKU-based with fixed dimensions and configurations. Customers cannot modify width, depth, height, drawer configuration, or cabinet structure. Only selectable variable is color/finish. Slab and 3DL collection: Built in-house. Intended to allow customization (primarily width adjustments). Positioned as either a lower-cost alternative to Shaker or a more design-flexible option. Catalog strategy: Phase 1: Launch SKU-based catalog for fast-moving projects (new builds, flips, remodels). Phase 2: Introduce custom catalog for clients requiring renderings, design consultations, and dimensional flexibility. Engineering requirements: Need clearly defined SKU names. Must document standard dimensions (e.g., base cabinets = 34.5" height industry standard). Clarify width increments per SKU. Define pantry and specialty cabinet dimensional structures (e.g., PC cabinets include width, height, and depth in SKU). Avoid guesswork by explicitly documenting all dimensional presets. Technical Issues & Fixes Spreadsheet adjustments required: Add product names corresponding to each SKU. Clearly define height and depth standards per cabinet type. Clarify pantry cabinet configurations (box vs. frame). Remove duplicate pricing entries where box and frame are listed separately if only box will be sold. Deactivate unused product types currently in the system (e.g., open cabinets not typically sold). Decisions Made Proceed with SKU-driven pricing model for initial rollout. Price differentiation is based strictly on door type: Shaker = fixed sale price per SKU. Slab = separate fixed price per SKU. No additional pricing complexity beyond door type difference at this stage. Custom cabinetry will not interfere with the initial SKU catalog. Follow-up meeting confirmed for next week at the same time. Challenges or Concerns Need to avoid rebuilding catalog structure later due to unclear requirements. Complexity of cabinetry variables requires thorough upfront definition. Engineering team requires complete dimensional data to build validation tables. Must ensure SKU structure aligns with how industry professionals interpret cabinet codes. Action Items Gabriel: Add product names for each SKU in the shared Google Sheet. Document standard heights and depths per cabinet type. Clarify pantry cabinet dimensional structure. Remove duplicate pantry box/frame pricing entries if selling box only. Add any additional SKU-related edge cases or special configurations. Carson: Schedule and prepare engineering review once updated spreadsheet is finalized. Send recap email with shared sheet link. Next Steps Gabriel to update spreadsheet with detailed dimensional standards and naming. Carson to coordinate meeting with engineer after spreadsheet updates. Phase 1 focus: Build and deploy SKU-based Shaker catalog. Phase 2: Develop separate custom catalog for Slab and 3DL products with adjustable widths and expanded options.

02/05/26 - Pickup meeting - https://app.fireflies.ai/view/Urbania-Cabinets-Allmoxy-Catch-Up::01KGMKTZPAMW9ZW26JQ1ZH13MB Agenda: Narrowed down to slab doors Meeting Summary Reconnected after a gap due to prior company closure and domain lapse; clarified current ownership and access. Discussed restarting the catalog build with a focused, simplified product offering. Agreed to initially offer full cabinets with slab doors only, excluding Shaker doors to avoid competing in a saturated, low-cost market. Goal is to target customers who value quality, reliability, and transparent pricing rather than lowest cost. Reviewed existing product templates in the system and discussed whether to retrofit them or build a new simplified master product. Agreed that simplicity and speed to launch are priorities, even if it means limiting options. Reviewed how pricing logic works at a component level (box, doors, drawers, hardware) rather than pricing each cabinet individually. Confirmed Mosaic is the downstream system informing parts and calculations. Walked through backend product attributes, proxy variables, and pricing rule concepts. Discussed operational items such as lead times, ship date logic, and user access. Created new user access due to expired domain and successfully logged in. Aligned on using a spreadsheet to define products, attributes, and pricing rules before engineering build. Key Takeaways Important Discussions Full cabinets will be offered, but only with slab doors initially. Shaker doors are intentionally excluded at launch to avoid price-driven competition. Quality differentiation will come from materials, drawer construction, and hardware options. Customers will be able to clearly see how upgrades (dovetail drawers, Blum hardware, materials) impact pricing. Existing catalog templates can be reused, simplified, or replaced depending on final requirements. Preference is to start with one “master” cabinet logic and clone/simplify as needed. Technical Issues & Fixes User login issues due to expired domain were resolved by creating a new user account. Confirmed access to the backend catalog and product configurations. Decisions Made Proceed with a simplified rule-based pricing model. Use slab doors as the only door style at launch. Offer multiple drawer box options (melamine, Baltic birch, dovetail, metal) as selectable upgrades. Pricing will be driven by component-level calculations (square footage, material cost, hardware cost). Use a spreadsheet as the primary input for engineering implementation. Keep configuration logic simple and avoid edge cases or custom exceptions. Challenges or Concerns Defining all attributes and pricing logic clearly upfront to avoid rework later. Balancing enough options to justify pricing differences without overcomplicating the build. Translating real-world cabinet construction and costs into clean, scalable pricing rules. Action Items Create a spreadsheet outlining: Products to be offered (base, wall, tall, etc.). All selectable attributes (box material, drawer box type, hardware, finishes, door type). Pricing logic for each attribute (square footage cost, fixed upcharge, percentage increase, etc.). Review existing products in the system to understand available configurations and possibilities. Ownership Spreadsheet creation: Ownership to be confirmed. Next Steps User to work on defining products, attributes, and pricing logic in a spreadsheet. Schedule a follow-up meeting next Thursday at the same time to review the spreadsheet. Hold an internal review before involving engineering to ensure requirements are clear and complete. After the call, a recording and concise recap will be sent to support follow-up work.

How an order moves through Allmoxy What is your current workflow? I will do a test order There is an expected workflow in Allmoxy Bid --> Ordered --> Verified --> In progress --> completed --> shipped When an order is verified, it is locked (the customer can no longer make changes) Customer's can make changes to Bids and Orders SHOW TRIGGERS AGAIN Test order Production lines/ work schedule report Production lines allow you to mimic what is happening on the floor in Allmoxy. What are the steps in making a slab door for example? Show Production Lines and Work Schedule Report (easy way to see jobs in verified status) We don't need to set up production lines, but it can be useful. We can even just make one category called "in progress". Or we can get more granular. (Show barcode scanning) You can start jobs for each production line --> moving them to in progress (which will drop off from the report) It will show you a start by date and a ship by date (based off lead time) From there, you can mimic what happens on the job floor in Allmoxy by using the scanning station OR you can move orders to in progress manually Shipping Methods How are they doing shipping? LTL Brokerage company They use multiple different companies Based off weight and volume They will add a shipping charge after LTL, then add that to open invoice Financial order settings (determine when your customers pay) Default checkout flow (use credit limit or pay before processing) . You can set this globally or per customer If some customers refuse to do pay before processing, you can change their individual checkout flow Credit limit is extending a certain amount of money to place an order, and set up payment terms (pay when they ship or the order is marked complete) Order limit/ build limit: the amount of product you will build but NOT necessarily ship to your customer. You set those terms Default interest rate- if you are doing terms and they haven't paid by the end of the month, a fee is attached. Daily is every day something is past due, it attaches a fee Sales tax presence Where are you doing business, just MI or regional? 5K a year threshold- when you collect 5K in revenue from a state, you need to start collecting sales tax Statement editor (credit limit): goes out to your customers at the end of every month if they have an outstanding balance. Onboarding #2 with Rigel Team 12/30/24 Tags These are ways you can group customers together for a certain purpose Cabinet dealers and contractors Pricing based on number of units over a 6 month time period Bronze, silver, gold, platinum (discount off retail price) These can be referenced in triggers and price adjustments Ex. you have a group of customers that are cabinet shops, and they get a certain discount. You can give this group of customers a "cabinet shop" tag on their company profile that can then be referenced later. You can also put tags on products How do you think you might group certain customers together? Price Adjustments Do you have customers that are priced differently than others? Why? Use price adjustments to achieve this Retail vs Wholesale Say you have a customer that is your oldest and most loyal customer, you always give them a 10% discount no matter what. Price adjustments are basically discounts or surcharges that can be applied to customers, groups of customers, or products. They are adjusted PER ITEM, not the total order amount Priority For when there are multiple price adjustments competing with one another If one discount has a higher priority than the other, the highest priority will override the other discount Ex. if you have a new customer discount and a summer sale discount going on at the same time, you would want the new customer discount to have a higher priority Tip: Use the Always setting, so you know if you are discounting or surcharging every time. You can also discount customers or products with certain tags Triggers How are you currently interacting with customers? Everything is manual (phone and emails) Triggers can automate that process for you Notify you, and your customers of something happening in Allmoxy Triggers to edit: 1, 6, 12, 16, 18, 19 Does he want to be notified of a bid? Or an order?
